lessons.title: ಸೋಮವಾರ to ಭಾನುವಾರ — the Sanskrit week
lessons.headword: ಸೋಮವಾರ ಮಂಗಳವಾರ ಬುಧವಾರ ಗುರುವಾರ ಶುಕ್ರವಾರ ಶನಿವಾರ ಭಾನುವಾರ
lessons.romanization: sōmavāra maṅgaḷavāra budhavāra guruvāra śukravāra śanivāra bhānuvāra
lessons.gloss: the seven weekdays — fully Sanskritic, like Hindi, but Sunday uses a DIFFERENT sun-name

segments.text: Unlike Tamil and Malayalam, Kannada's week is built entirely from Sanskrit — the same recipe as Hindi's. But even here, one day picks a different Sanskrit word than Hindi does.

blocks.title: You'll want to know: The pattern: [deity] + ವಾರ, "day"

utterances: Kannada: ಸೋಮವಾರ (Somavāra). deity/planet: Moon (Soma). day: Monday.
Kannada: ಮಂಗಳವಾರ (Maṅgaḷavāra). deity/planet: Mars (Maṅgala). day: Tuesday.
Kannada: ಬುಧವಾರ (Budhavāra). deity/planet: Mercury (Budha). day: Wednesday.
Kannada: ಗುರುವಾರ (Guruvāra). deity/planet: Jupiter (Guru/Bṛhaspati). day: Thursday.
Kannada: ಶುಕ್ರವಾರ (Śukravāra). deity/planet: Venus (Śukra). day: Friday.
Kannada: ಶನಿವಾರ (Śanivāra). deity/planet: Saturn (Śani). day: Saturday.
Kannada: ಭಾನುವಾರ (Bhānuvāra). deity/planet: the Sun (Bhānu, "light, splendor"). day: Sunday.

segments.text: Five of these are identical in shape to Hindi's — same deity, same ‑vāra/ ‑vār ending. Sunday is the interesting exception: where Hindi says रविवार (Ravivār, from Ravi, "sun"), Kannada says ಭಾನುವಾರ (Bhānuvāra), built on a different Sanskrit word for the sun — Bhānu, "light, splendor," rather than Ravi. Sanskrit has many names for the sun, and different languages downstream picked different ones for their week.

segments.instruction: "Somavāra, Maṅgaḷavāra, Budhavāra, Guruvāra, Śukravāra, Śanivāra" — Monday through Saturday
segments.source: [YOU SAY: "Somavāra, Maṅgaḷavāra, Budhavāra, Guruvāra, Śukravāra, Śanivāra" — Monday through Saturday]

segments.instruction: the contrast — Hindi says Ravivāra (Ravi), Kannada says Bhānuvāra (Bhānu) — two different Sanskrit sun-names
segments.source: [YOU SAY: the contrast — Hindi says Ravivāra (Ravi), Kannada says Bhānuvāra (Bhānu) — two different Sanskrit sun-names]

segments.text: What ending does every Kannada weekday share, and where's it from? (‑ವಾರ -vāra, Sanskrit "day.") Which day differs from Hindi's version, and how? (Sunday — Kannada's Bhānuvāra ("light") uses a different Sanskrit sun-name than Hindi's Ravivār ("Ravi").)

lessons.title: ◌ೋ (ō) — one character, met inside words you already say
lessons.gloss: the single character ೋ — recognised inside words you already say

needs: a pen and something to write on
your eyes, for letter shapes on the page
notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your hands, so it is not a driving lesson. You will want a pen and something to write on and your eyes, for letter shapes on the page. You can listen to everything else now. I will say so again when we reach them, but leave these sections until you have stopped: Script you'll notice: ◌ೋ and Guided Practice.

segments.text: Before the new one: ಡ — what does it do?
One character this time. Just one — and you have been saying it for pages without knowing which mark on the page it was.
It is a vowel sign. It is not a letter and never stands alone: it attaches to a consonant and replaces the a built into it with ō. Replaces, not adds — the a is gone.
You already say these, and every one of them has ◌ೋ (ō) somewhere inside it:
ಸಂತೋಷ santōṣa — joy / pleased to meet you.
ಹೋಗು hōgu — to go (and ಬಾ, come).
ಹೋಗಿ ಬರುತ್ತೇನೆ hōgi baruttēne — goodbye (lit. "I'll go and come back").
ನಾಳೆ ಸಿಗೋಣ nāḷe sigōṇa — see you tomorrow.
Put your pen on ◌ೋ (ō) and follow its line. Copy the shape you can see — slowly, and larger than it is printed.

This book does not yet tell you where to start the character or which way to travel. That is a real thing, taught with real variation from school to school, and it is not written down here until it can be written down with a source. Copying what is in front of you needs no such source, and it is how the shape gets into your hand in the meantime.

segments.instruction: at these words, and find ◌ೋ (ō) in the ones that have it
segments.source: [YOU LOOK: at these words, and find ◌ೋ in the ones that have it]

segments.text: ಸಂತೋಷ, ಹೋಗು, ನಮಸ್ಕಾರ.

segments.instruction: ◌ೋ three times, saying ō as you finish each one
segments.source: [YOU TRACE: ◌ೋ three times, saying *ō* as you finish each one]

segments.instruction: back at any page of this chapter and find ◌ೋ (ō) once more

segments.text: Which character is this — ◌ೋ? What vowel does it put on the consonant it attaches to — and what does it take off? (Puts ō on; takes the built-in a off.) Name one word you already say that contains it.

lessons.title: ೨ (2) — the digit for eraḍu
lessons.gloss: the Kannada digit 2, met on top of a word already learned

needs: a pen and something to write on
your eyes, for letter shapes on the page
notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your hands, so it is not a driving lesson. You will want a pen and something to write on and your eyes, for letter shapes on the page. You can listen to everything else now. I will say so again when we reach them, but leave these sections until you have stopped: Script you'll notice: ೨ and Guided Practice.

segments.text: Before the new shape: ೧ — which number is it?
One digit this time, and you already know its name.
೨ — 2, the digit for ಎರಡು (eraḍu), "two".
Each Dravidian script carries its own set of ten digits. Telugu, Malayalam and Tamil all have theirs; none of the four sets is borrowed from another.
Follow the numbered strip: start where movement 1 begins, and let each panel show you the next movement before your pen makes it. Then write ೨ (2) yourself — slowly, and larger than it is printed.

The strip shows where to start the character and which way to travel, in one attested order. That is taught with real variation from school to school, so the strip names its source beneath it: treat it as a sound way in, not the only one.

segments.instruction: at the digits you have met, and name each one aloud

segments.text: Which number is ೨? (2 — eraḍu, ಎರಡು.) Name every digit you have met so far, in order.

segments.text: (Sōmavāra, maṅgaḷavāra, budhavāra, guruvāra, śukravāra, śanivāra, bhānuvāra.)
What ending does every day share, and what does it mean? (-vāra, "day.")
Which day takes a different Sanskrit sun-name from Hindi's, and what are the two names? (Sunday: Kannada bhānuvāra, "light"; Hindi ravivār.)
ಸೋಮವಾರ is Monday. Which mark in it gives its first consonant the ō, and what does that mark take away? (◌ೋ: it puts ō on and takes the built-in a off.)
Which number is ೨, and which word does it stand for? (2, eraḍu.)
